title: AWS Performance Fundamentals
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose of aws performance fundamentals and its relationship to Performance Optimization and Cloud Cost Management.
Interpret the example and identify at least one prerequisite or boundary relevant to aws performance fundamentals.
Propose a safe verification or troubleshooting step and record one security, reliability or cost consideration.

content.intro: In this lesson, you will learn aws performance fundamentals in the context of Performance Optimization and Cloud Cost Management. You will connect the listed subtopics to a practical decision, inspect a small example, and define evidence that would confirm or disprove your assumptions.
content.why_it_matters: AWS Performance Fundamentals matters because it is one part of performance and cost management. Real workloads depend on explicit prerequisites, correct permissions, predictable behavior and a way to verify outcomes. Learning the decision points helps you distinguish a working demonstration from a safe and supportable design.

content_blocks.title: Module 19: Performance Optimization and Cloud Cost Management
content_blocks.alt_text: Five-step overview for module 19, Performance Optimization and Cloud Cost Management, followed by verification, least-privilege security, recovery, and cost-cleanup checks.
content_blocks.caption: Module 19 learning sequence: understand the concept, make a controlled design/configuration, verify behavior, and document security/reliability/cost trade-offs.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text:
**Core idea.** AWS Performance Fundamentals belongs to Performance Optimization and Cloud Cost Management. Measure performance and cost against a workload goal. Use actual usage and cost data, right-size gradually, and remember that a budget alert is not a spending cap.

The PDF lists these subtopics: Latency and throughput; Resource utilization; Bottleneck identification; Workload performance requirements. Treat them as a connected workflow rather than a list to memorize. Start with the workload requirement, identify the AWS resource/control involved, and write down who owns configuration and operation.

content_blocks.title: Practical reasoning
content_blocks.text: **Apply it safely.** For aws performance fundamentals, name the prerequisites and the expected result before making a change. Prefer a read-only inspection or local/static example first. Then plan a normal case, a failure case, and a verification step. In a live account, require the account owner-approved sandbox, narrow permissions, spend visibility and cleanup plan. Do not put credentials in code or commit local configuration files.

items.title: Latency and throughput
items.text: Identify the AWS resource or design decision involved, the permissions and prerequisites it needs, and the evidence that shows it is configured as intended.

items.title: Resource utilization
items.text: Compare the available option with the workload requirement; record the operational, security, availability and cost trade-offs rather than assuming one option is always best.

items.title: Bottleneck identification
items.text: Write a verification step and a failure case. For hands-on work, start with read-only inspection and use an approved sandbox before changing cloud resources.

items.title: Workload performance requirements
items.text: Record ownership, dependencies and teardown/recovery behavior so the design can be operated safely after the first successful test.

content_blocks.title: Query measured AWS costs: AWS Performance Fundamentals
content_blocks.code:
# Read-only example related to: AWS Performance Fundamentals
aws ce get-cost-and-usage --time-period Start=2026-10-01,End=2026-10-11 --granularity DAILY --metrics UnblendedCost
content_blocks.expected_output: Cost and usage results for the selected complete date range, subject to account permissions and Cost Explorer data availability.
content_blocks.run_instructions: This block is an inspectable example, not an AWS action performed by CodeLeaf. For the read-only CLI command, first configure the named profile through an approved credential provider, verify identity, replace example identifiers when required and inspect current official CLI documentation. Do not apply/deploy changes in a real account without account-owner approval, least-privilege permissions and a reviewed cost/cleanup plan.
content_blocks.reset_steps: No AWS resource is created by this lesson example. If you independently run an approved lab, capture the starting state first, follow the lab-specific teardown instructions, check dependent resources and billing/resource inventories, and document anything retained.
content_blocks.limitations: The CodeLeaf playground is an HTML/CSS/JavaScript preview and does not execute AWS APIs, shell commands, SQL or cloud deployments. Treat output as illustrative; live values depend on credentials, permissions, Region, service state and schema.

content_blocks.title: Security and cost checkpoint
content_blocks.text: For cost work, a budget notification is not a hard spending cap. Check actual usage and remove approved lab resources.

task: Create a one-page decision card for “AWS Performance Fundamentals”. State the goal, prerequisites, the AWS resource or control involved, the expected result, one read-only/static verification step, one failure case, the relevant permission boundary, and cost/cleanup considerations. Do not create or alter billable resources unless the account owner has approved the lab.
hints: Start from the exact subtopics in the lesson and define the desired state in your own words.
Prefer a read-only check or static artifact before a mutating command; record the identity/Region and required permissions.
Verify the expected result and a failure path using current official documentation; write down cost and cleanup implications.
expected_output: A short reviewable decision card for AWS Performance Fundamentals with prerequisites, evidence, a failure case, security implications and cost/cleanup notes.

common_mistakes.problem: Treating one successful example as proof of production readiness.
common_mistakes.why: The example may not test permissions, regional/service prerequisites, retries, recovery, quotas or edge cases.
common_mistakes.fix: Write acceptance criteria, test a failure path, inspect logs/state and record the limits of the result.

common_mistakes.problem: Changing a live resource before confirming its effect and cost.
common_mistakes.why: Cloud changes can expose data, break traffic or leave billable dependencies behind.
common_mistakes.fix: Start read-only, use an approved sandbox, review the change, tag ownership and verify cleanup.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying broad permissions or credentials into source files.
common_mistakes.why: Broad permissions and leaked long-lived credentials increase the impact of mistakes.
common_mistakes.fix: Use scoped roles/temporary credentials, keep secrets in approved stores and review access boundaries.

summary: AWS Performance Fundamentals is taught as part of Performance Optimization and Cloud Cost Management.
Measure performance and cost against a workload goal. Use actual usage and cost data, right-size gradually, and remember that a budget alert is not a spending cap.
Verify assumptions with official service documentation and evidence from the relevant AWS resource, logs or tests.
For live labs, confirm permissions and likely charges before acting, then verify cleanup.
